passage: Come, sit, and I will tell you what my first office taught me. I was twenty-four then, and the nameplate said Swati Rao. A woman called Deepika sat at the next desk. She greeted the guard by name every morning and brought sweets on birthdays. But when the lunch table started picking apart a colleague's marriage, Deepika said lightly, "I will pass, tell me when the food comes," and went on eating. No speech, no frown. Two others went quiet too, though Mahesh kept talking a little. Nobody stopped inviting her. The following week I tried her line myself, and my voice shook only a little.

qa.q: What did Deepika say when the lunch table started picking apart a colleague's marriage?
qa.a: Deepika said lightly, "I will pass, tell me when the food comes," and went on eating.

qa.q: What might Deepika have been feeling while she declined with no speech and no frown?
qa.a: Deepika seems calm and unbothered, without needing to win or condemn anyone; going on eating suggests she was comfortable dissenting.

qa.q: What did Swati take from Deepika that helped when trying it the next week?
qa.a: Swati used Deepika's light line and did not lecture anyone, which made saying no small enough to try even with a shaky voice.

qa.q: How might it have felt for Deepika when the table went quiet after "I will pass"?
qa.a: Deepika may have felt a small flicker of worry about the silence, but the daily invitations that followed show the group accepted it.

grounding: A mature young adult keeps courtesy but politely declines gossip, dissenting calmly without needing to win, told as an elder's memory.

passage: Fifteen minutes before the auditors arrived, the pantry was crowded and the lights kept flickering. Kunal filled tea cups for the visitors, the way he always did, thanking the cleaner as he passed. Yamini, stirring sugar, lowered her voice: "Did you hear why Rekha is on leave? Apparently..." Two people leaned in. A third, Vikram, studied the biscuit tin. Kunal kept pouring. "I would rather not talk about Rekha," he said mildly. "Can we check the cash register figures before they come?" Yamini shrugged and laughed, "Fine, boss." The lights flickered again, and Kunal carried the tray out first.

qa.q: How many minutes remained before the auditors arrived?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes remained before the auditors arrived.

qa.q: Why does Kunal keep pouring tea and answer so mildly when Yamini starts gossiping?
qa.a: Kunal wants to decline the gossip without a fight; the mild tone and the change of topic suggest calm, not a wish to condemn Yamini.

qa.q: What made Kunal's refusal easy for the group to accept?
qa.a: Kunal offered a useful alternative, checking the cash register figures, and did not criticise Yamini, so nobody had to lose face.

qa.q: What might Vikram be feeling while studying the biscuit tin during the gossip?
qa.a: Vikram may feel uncomfortable, unwilling to join in but also unwilling to speak up, so looking away is a way of staying out of it.

grounding: A young adult follows courtesy norms such as serving tea but politely declines gossip, without needing to win or condemn.

passage:
In his first month at the Bengaluru software office, Jagdish learned the unwritten rules fast. Everyone greeted the security guard by name. Everyone stayed for the four o'clock chai round. Birthdays meant a cake and a card, even for people you barely knew. He followed all of it gladly.
Then one afternoon, over chai, Rakesh lowered his voice. “Heard why Ayesha from design got moved? Her manager said—”
Jagdish stirred his tea. “I'd rather not guess about her. She's not here to say her side.” He said it mildly and asked Rakesh about the cricket score.
There was a small pause. Then Pooja laughed and talked about the match too. Later Ayesha herself joined the chai round, and Jagdish poured her a cup.

qa.q: What time was the chai round?
qa.a: It was at four o'clock.

qa.q: How can you tell Jagdish felt calm when he declined the gossip?
qa.a: He said it mildly, kept stirring his tea and switched to the cricket score, so he seemed steady and not angry at anyone.

qa.q: What does Jagdish's approach do well?
qa.a: He keeps the friendly norms like chai and birthdays but quietly steps out of gossip, without lecturing or making the group feel bad.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt after the pause?
qa.a: He might have felt a little awkward, but since Jagdish moved on to the match, he wasn't shamed in front of others.

grounding: Shows a young adult who follows courteous office norms but calmly declines gossip without condemning the group.

passage:
“Seema, you're in for the Navratri decorations, right? Everyone brings one string of lights,” said Mrs Kulkarni at the society committee meeting.
“Of course. I'll bring two.”
“Good. Now,” Gargi leaned in, “has anyone seen the new tenants in B-wing? Not married, I hear. Coming home at midnight.”
A few heads turned to Seema. She smiled. “I haven't met them yet. I'll probably just say hello at the garba.”
“But don't you think—”
“Honestly, Gargi, I'd rather not decide anything about them. Should we fix the rangoli roster?”
Mrs Kulkarni laughed. “Yes, the rangoli. Seema, you take Saturday.”
“Done,” Seema said, writing it down.

qa.q: How many strings of lights did Seema offer to bring?
qa.a: She offered to bring two.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling while leaning in about the tenants?
qa.a: Gargi seemed curious and eager for gossip, keen to share the rumour.

qa.q: Which choice by Seema worked, and why?
qa.a: She happily joined the shared decorations but politely stepped away from the gossip and moved to the rangoli roster, so nobody was insulted.

qa.q: How might the new tenants be affected by the way this meeting went?
qa.a: Because Seema refused to judge them, they may get a friendly hello at the garba instead of arriving to rumours.

grounding: Shows a young woman who follows the society's courteous norms but calmly declines gossip without condemning anyone.

passage:
When I, Salma, joined the school as a new science teacher last year, the staffroom had its own rules.
Some I took up at once. Everyone stood when the senior teachers entered. Everyone shared their tiffin at lunch. You never took the corner chair, which was Mrs Iyer's. Those rules made the place feel kind.
Other rules I let go. At lunch, talk would often turn to Himani, the young music teacher, and what she wore. I would smile and ask someone about their class trip instead. Once Mr Pinto said, “Salma, you never have an opinion.” I said, “Not on her clothes, no,” and passed him my pickle. He laughed.
By March, the Himani talk had grown quieter. I don't know if I caused that. I only know I slept easier.

qa.q: Whose chair was the corner chair?
qa.a: It was Mrs Iyer's.

qa.q: How did Salma feel about the staffroom's gossip?
qa.a: Salma felt uncomfortable with it but calm, and slept easier for staying out of it without making a fuss.

qa.q: What could a new teacher learn from Salma's way of handling the staffroom?
qa.a: Keep the rules that make a place kind, like standing for seniors and sharing lunch, and change the subject lightly when talk turns unkind.

qa.q: How might Himani be affected if more teachers acted like Salma?
qa.a: She would likely feel more respected and less talked about, and might fit into the staffroom more easily.

grounding: A young teacher sorts staffroom norms, keeping courtesies and calmly declining gossip, without needing to win or condemn anyone.

Note for Dolma's three-month review, from the floor supervisor.
Dolma has settled into the accounts team well. She follows the team's small customs without fuss: she joins the Monday tea round, remembered Lokesh's birthday with a card, and keeps the shared printer tidy.
On Thursday I saw something else. At lunch, Kavya and Lokesh started on the new trainee's "attitude" and turned to Dolma for agreement. Dolma said, "I haven't worked with her enough to say. Has anyone asked her?" and went back to her rice. No lecture, no sulking. Kavya looked put out; Lokesh changed the subject. Dolma still sat with them the next day.
What I did next: in our one-to-one I told Dolma I had noticed and asked whether she felt pressured. She said, "A bit. But I'd rather be the boring one at lunch." I will keep an ear on how the trainee is talked about.

qa.q: What did Dolma say when Kavya and Lokesh wanted agreement about the trainee?
qa.a: Dolma said, "I haven't worked with her enough to say. Has anyone asked her?"

qa.q: How did Dolma feel about stepping out of the lunch gossip?
qa.a: Dolma felt a little pressured and uncomfortable, yet calm and settled about the choice, as "I'd rather be the boring one at lunch" shows.

qa.q: What does Dolma's approach get right about group customs?
qa.a: Dolma keeps the kind customs like the tea round and the birthday card, declines only the gossip, and does it without preaching or leaving the group.

qa.q: How might Kavya have experienced Dolma's reply?
qa.a: Kavya may have felt awkward and a bit checked, since the easy agreement did not come, but nobody was attacked, so the table could carry on.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps courteous team customs, politely declines gossip, and dissents calmly without condemning the group.
